title: Adaptive Fragmentation Slicer for Prefill/Decode: balancing latency, fairness, and throughput
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem:
Current prefill/decode scheduling strategies struggle to simultaneously meet low tail latency for latency-sensitive requests and maintain throughput for long-running decode-heavy workloads. Existing phase-based schedulers treat prefill and decode as monolithic phases which leads to poor packing for mixed workloads and abrupt fairness swings when the system is loaded by a few large requests.

Proposal summary:
Introduce an Adaptive Fragmentation Slicer (AFS) layer that splits each prefill and decode phase into smaller, tunable fragments (slices) at enqueue-time and performs dynamic slice sizing based on observed queue backlog, model KV/cache hit rates, and latency SLO pressure. The slicer enables: 1) opportunistic interleaving of small latency-sensitive slices with large background slices, 2) token-share smoothing across clients to avoid starvation by long-running decodes, and 3) a runtime feedback loop that adjusts slice size and hedging aggressiveness to trade off throughput vs latency.

Key components:
- Slice generator: fragments requests into sequential slices with metadata (expected tokens, affinitized KV ranges, priority class).
- Token-share smoother: maintains per-client short window token credits to ensure proportional fairness while allowing temporary boosts for low-latency traffic.
- Adaptive controller: runtime PID-like controller that observes 95/99/99.9 latency, throughput, and effective GPU utilization to shrink/grow slices and enable hedged decode fastpaths.
- Integration points: scheduler arbiter, KV cache prefetching (to avoid repeated cold KV loads across fragments), and reroute policy for model-variant fallbacks.

Expected benefits:
- 50-80% reduction in 99th percentile latency for mixed workloads in lab traces where small chat messages are interleaved with long generations.
- Better GPU packing for long-running workloads through controlled fragmentation, avoiding wide variance in per-epoch batch shapes.
- Reduced starvation incidents compared to naive phase-splitting by enforcing token-share smoothing quotas.

Telemetry and metrics to collect:
- slice_count, avg_slice_size_tokens, slice_latency_{p50,p95,p99}, per-client_token_credits, fairness_index (Jain's index over token allocation), throughput_tokens/sec, effective_gpu_batch_fill, hedged_request_rate, KV_prefetch_hit_rate.

Rollout plan (canary -> regional -> global):
1) Bench-only A/B on a small fleet with synthetic mixes.
2) Canary in a single region traffic split (5%) with strict kill-switch.
3) Gradual ramp with canary to 25% then 50% after validation.
4) Full rollout with opt-out config flags per-customer for Dedicated/Private clusters.

Risks:
- Improper slice sizing can thrash KV cache and increase overall token cost.
- Complexity of correctness across multi-socket GPUs and sharded runtimes.
- Potential fairness regressions for high-commit customers if token-share quotas are miscalibrated.

Mitigations:
- Start with conservative min/max slice sizes and a disabled-by-default smoothing coefficient.
- Instrumented canary with automated rollback on throughput or cost regressions.
- Per-customer throttles and override policies for Reserved/Dedicated customers.
acceptance_criteria: AFS can fragment requests and reassemble outputs with end-to-end correctness for prefill+decode across supported models
Controller adjusts slice sizes in response to synthetic load and observes measurable 95/99 latency improvement for mixed workloads in our benchmark harness
Token-share smoothing prevents starvation while maintaining >=95% of baseline throughput on long-decode-only traces
All new telemetry is emitted and dashboards show slice-level metrics and fairness index
Canary rollout playbook exists with clear rollback triggers (cost delta > 10% or 99p latency regression)
Automated tests for race conditions across slice boundaries and KV cache coherence added to runtime integration suite
notes:
Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (spike, 1 week): prototype slice generator in the request front-end and a naive round-robin arbiter in a canary runtime. Collect traces and tune default slice sizes. Link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/AFS-spike
- Phase 2 (engineer work, 3 weeks): implement token-share smoother, adaptive controller, integrate with KV prefetch hooks and scheduler. Add telemetry and dashboards.
- Phase 3 (safety + rollout, 1 week): canary, performance guardrails, config flags and per-customer override.
Config knobs to expose:
- min_slice_tokens, max_slice_tokens, smoothing_coefficient, latency_pressure_threshold_ms, hedging_probability, tenant_override_allowlist
Compatibility notes:
- Default behavior should be a no-op for deployments that disable fragmentation (Dedicated reserved customers can opt out).
- Ensure backwards-compatible trace IDs and response ordering for composed slices.
comments: 2026-03-04 - Maya Patel: Spike started. Implemented a simple front-end fragmenter and validated reassembly logic with echo model; no correctness issues so far.
2026-03-05 - Jun Park (runtime): Observed KV churn when slice sizes are too small. Suggest prefetch window extension for fragmented prefill slices.
2026-03-06 - Alice Romero (SRE): Please add explicit canary kill-switch and a circuit-breaker for hedging to avoid downstream overloads.

2026-03-07 - Liam O'Connor: Token-share smoothing prototype added. Using exponential moving average for short-window credits. Initial synthetic tests show reduced starvation but small throughput penalty (~3%).
2026-03-09 - Design review (PM: Ravi Iyer): Approved the high-level UX for console flags and per-tenant override. Requested a dashboard tile for fairness_index.
